per_object_cap.stated: not applicable: the unit is a session, not an object

interface_detail: a notebook in the browser; no SSH and no inbound port
tooling: Jupyter; the Colab client; no shell beyond the notebook's
chaining: a notebook is not a machine: nothing survives the runtime, so it cannot hold state or serve
limits_note: a documented absence: 'Colab does not publish these limits' is a discretionary throttle, not a quota
reliability_note: Colab states outright that it prioritises interactive users and that runtimes time out when idle, so a long job is cut for reasons the client cannot see

free_tier.stated: free of charge access to computing resources including GPUs and TPUs; a notebook runs for at most 12 hours; usage limits, idle timeout, maximum VM lifetime and GPU types are not published and vary over time
free_tier.notes: There is no published GPU-hour number. Anything quoted for Colab's free GPU quota is somebody's recollection.

retention.stated: the VM disk is deleted when the runtime is recycled; only Google Drive survives

egress.terms: no published egress allowance or price for the notebook runtime

limits.value: an unpublished, fluctuating usage limit on GPU and total compute

identity_cost.detail: a Google account; no card for the free tier

evidence.proved: in the free version notebooks can run for at most 12 hours, depending on availability and usage patterns
'Colab does not publish these limits, in part because they can vary over time'
virtual machines are deleted when idle for a while and have a maximum lifetime enforced by the service

'In the version of Colab that is free of charge notebooks can run for at most 12 hours, depending on availability and your usage patterns', with 'Colab does not publish these limits, in part because they can vary over time' and 'access to expensive resources like GPUs is heavily restricted', all quoted
quoted: 'In the version of Colab that is free of charge notebooks can run for at most 12 hours, depending on availability and your usage patterns.'
quoted: 'Colab does not publish these limits, in part because they can vary over time.'
quoted: 'Virtual machines are deleted when idle for a while, and have a maximum lifetime enforced by the Colab service.'
quoted: 'Colab prioritizes interactive compute. Runtimes will time out if you are idle.'
quoted: 'In the version of Colab that is free of charge you are able to access VMs with a standard system memory profile.' — no number is given
quoted: 'on higher plans, additional capabilities such as background execution' — background execution is a paid-plan feature, so the free tier cannot run unattended

notes: RAM, GPU class and the idle timeout are all unpublished, so no record can carry them. What would settle them is running a probe notebook that reports /proc/meminfo and nvidia-smi, which needs an account.

shape.note: the vendor publishes no numbers; GPU type 'varies over time'

session_cap.note: 12 h cap; idle timeout and VM lifetime unpublished

extras.unattended_mechanism: none on the free tier; background execution is listed as a paid-plan capability
extras.units: RAM and disk are quoted in the vendor's own decimal GB, not GiB. The ram_gib and disk_gib keys carry the vendor's number unconverted, so where a vendor writes 30 GB the key holds 30 and the true value is about 27.9 GiB. No conversion was performed.

binding_note: the quota is real but unquantified, so it cannot be planned against; the 12-hour wall is the only number the vendor will commit to
confidence_note: the 12-hour cap and the refusal to publish the rest are quoted from the vendor FAQ. RAM and GPU class are unverified because the page states a 'standard memory profile' without a number.
